newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss historians urge study on ties to Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Swiss historians urge study on ties to Nazis.

text.p: Leading Swiss historians called on Tuesday for a closer look at the country's largely unexplored role as a black market for Nazi loot and its importance as a financier to Hitler's war effort.

Swiss business with the Axis powers surrounding it during World War Two is well documented, but it remains unclear how much Swiss money and material helped Germany continue its war effort until defeat in 1945, they told a government-sponsored seminar.

Across town, Berne officials met leaders of the World Jewish Congress (WJC) and representatives of Swiss business to discuss creation of a Holocaust memorial fund to be financed by contributions from banks and other corporate pillars.
"All of the parties expressed the desire to see the Special Fund established as rapidly as possible," the foreign ministry said in a statement after two days of talks.

Representatives of Israel's prime minister, the World Jewish Restitution Organisation, Swiss Jews, gypsy groups and business leaders also took part in Tuesday's talks between Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti and WJC Secretary General Israel Singer.
WJC Assistant Secretary General Maram Stern said after a round of talks on Monday night that his group, which has led a campaign for the fund, saw no big problems over who will run it.

Galvanised by international pressure and threats of losing business, big Swiss banks have already contributed 100 million Swiss francs ($68.5 million) to the fund, which is being coordinated by the Swiss government in Berne.
Swiss machinery makers said they would support it.
But Stern suggested the memorial fund should be combined with a broader humanitarian foundation the government has proposed and which would draw on federal funds.
The public foundation must await the first findings later this year of a historians' panel now reviewing Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre, the government has said.

Berne will then decide what steps may be appropriate to make amends for Switzerland's economic collaboration with Nazi Germany and its anti-Jewish wartime immigration policy that turned back thousands of Jewish refugees as the Holocaust raged.

Historians at the Berne seminar said the extent to which the Nazis used neutral Switzerland's status as a financial centre untouched by the war to sell or hoard cash, gold, jewels and securities seized from Jews and other victims was still unclear.
"It is urgent and important that this research be undertaken," said Marc Perrenoud, an expert on Swiss financial relations with Nazi Germany and Mussolini's Italy.
The Swiss government in December launched a major historical inquiry into the country's wartime past, and the seminar was designed to take stock of what still left to be probed.

Perrenoud said while Berne froze German assets in Switzerland near the end of the war under pressure from the Allied powers, it was not clear to him whether all stolen goods had ever been returned to the rightful owners.
"After looking through the Swiss Federal Archives, there is cause to doubt this (return)," he said.

Federal Archives director Christoph Graf said historians had once thought Switzerland's role in financing and supplying the German war effort was marginal, but were increasingly viewing it as a major help for Hitler.

Germany and Italy pressured tiny Switzerland into extending credits during the war, transported strategic supplies such as coal through the Swiss Alps, bought material from Swiss companies and frequently used Swiss banks.
"But the theory that the war lasted two years longer because of Swiss financial and economic assistance is no more than a hypothesis now, although it cannot be dismissed," he said.

Gian Trepp, who has written extensively about German wartime sales of gold it stole from occupied countries' central banks, said one murky area was the movement of other Nazi loot through Switzerland.
Trepp said little was known about the extent to which the German state and individual Nazis used Switzerland as a black market to unload treasures seized from concentration camp prisoners and others.

"It must be assumed that there was a market in Switzerland for stolen gold, jewels, stocks and bonds and so on," he said, noting that Switzerland had intact banks, businesses and bourses and an easily convertible currency during the war.
"This market must be studied. As far as I am aware, this has not been done," he added.
